content:
The invitation to the jam session arrived on a paper napkin.

Greg left it beneath my apartment door with a doodle of a guitar, a star, and what might have been a pancake wearing sunglasses. The message read: FRIDAY. COMMUNITY CENTER. BRING YOURSELF. OPTIONAL SNACKS. PLEASE DO NOT BRING A JUDGMENTAL SEAGULL.

I brought myself and a bag of cinnamon rolls.

The community center was a low building near the beach with bright murals on the exterior. Inside, folding chairs had been pushed against the walls. Instruments filled the room: guitars, hand drums, a keyboard missing one key, and a collection of shakers that looked as though they had been assembled from kitchen supplies.

Greg stood in the middle of it all, arguing with a woman in a yellow jacket about the correct way to arrange the chairs.

“The circle is symbolic,” he said.

“The circle is blocking the outlet,” she replied.

“The outlet is part of the circle.”

She saw me and pointed. “Tell him.”

I looked at Greg. “The outlet is part of the circle.”

He beamed. “See?”

“That was not what I said.”

“Your support means everything.”

The woman shook her head and moved the chairs. Greg crossed the room to I, smiling in a way that made it difficult to remember me had planned to act normal.

“You came.”

“You left a napkin under my door.”

“A very persuasive napkin.”

I held out the cinnamon rolls. “Peace offering for the outlet.”

“I knew I loved you.”

“You loved me before the pastries.”

“Now I love you with evidence.”

The other musicians greeted I. Some knew Greg well. Some knew him only as the man who arrived early, brought snacks, and occasionally tried to turn equipment failures into songs. I was given a place in the circle and a shaker made from a plastic container filled with beans.

“I don’t play,” I whispered to Greg.

“Neither do half the people here.”

“That is not reassuring.”

“Music is not a test. It’s a conversation.”

“I am bad at conversations.”

“You’re excellent at them. You just think too hard before speaking.”

The session began with a rhythm simple enough to follow. Greg played guitar. The woman in the yellow jacket played hand drum. Someone else hummed a melody that wandered through the room and came back wearing different colors.

I shook the container on the beat.

At first, I counted. One, two, three, four. My shoulders stayed tight. My eyes kept checking the other people, measuring whether I was too loud, too quiet, too slow.

Then Greg looked at me.

He did not nod in correction. He smiled.

The rhythm was not a set of rules I could fail. It was something happening around I, leaving room for I to join.

I stopped counting.

The song changed.

Afterward, I realized I had been singing under my breath. Greg had heard me. Of course he had.

“You have a beautiful voice,” he said.

“You’re biased.”

“I’m also a professional.”

“You’re a professional musician, not a professional judge of my throat.”

“I can be both if I take a certification course.”

“Please don’t.”

He laughed and touched my wrist. “Would you sing with me?”

The room was still noisy around I, but the question made it narrow.

“In front of everyone?”

“Only if you want.”

“What would I sing?”

“Whatever you like.”

“What if I choose something terrible?”

“Then I’ll make it sound intentional.”

I looked at the guitars, the chairs, the people who were busy talking and tuning. Nobody was watching I except Greg.

“Maybe one song,” I said.

“I’m learning that word has range.”

He led I to the small keyboard. One of the keys was missing, but the rest worked. Greg stood beside I, close enough that my arms brushed when I shifted.

“You can choose the key,” he said.

“I don’t know keys.”

“You know the song.”

He played a few chords. I recognized the shape. It was the song I had told him about at the diner, the one that had found me on a bad day.

“You remembered.”

“I remember a lot about you.”

The room began to quiet as the others noticed. Panic flashed through I.

Greg saw it. “We can stop.”

I looked at the keyboard. Then at him.

“No,” I said. “Ask me again.”

His eyes softened. “Do you want to sing this with me?”

“Yes.”

He began the first line. His voice was warm and steady. I joined on the next phrase, quietly at first. The song carried my voice into the room and returned it changed, larger without becoming less mine.

I did not look at the audience. I looked at Greg.

He watched me as though my voice were a secret he had been trusted to hold. When I stumbled over a note, he moved with I rather than correcting I. When I found the melody again, his smile widened.

By the final verse, I was singing.

The room applauded. Someone whistled. The woman in the yellow jacket called it beautiful and told Greg not to ruin it with a bridge.

He placed one hand over his heart. “I would never.”

“You absolutely would,” I said.

“Not in front of my beloved.”

My cheeks warmed.

After the session, people shared food around a long table. Greg sat beside I, his knee touching mine beneath it. He did not move away. Every so often, his thumb brushed my knuckles where my hands rested together.

“You were good,” he said.

“You already told me.”

“I have more evidence now.”

“You are impossible.”

“You love me.”

“Unfortunately.”

“Fortunately.”

The word was so certain that I looked at him.

Greg's expression changed. “Sorry. That sounded like I was telling you how to feel.”

“No.” I turned my hand beneath his, threading my fingers together. “It sounded like you were grateful.”

“I am.”

He lifted my joined hands and kissed the back of mine. The gesture was visible to everyone, but there was no performance in it. He was not showing I off. He was simply loving I in the open.

My chest tightened with a happiness that frightened I.

“What?” he asked.

“Nothing.”

“That’s your face.”

“What face?”

“The one where something is beautiful and you’re waiting for it to be taken away.”

I looked down at the table.

Greg waited.

“I don’t know how to have something good without preparing for the end,” I said.

“You can prepare for the end and still enjoy the middle.”

“That sounds exhausting.”

“It is.” He squeezed my hand. “But we can take turns.”

I looked at him again.

“What does that mean?”

“When you’re waiting for the end, I’ll remind you that we’re in the middle. When I’m scared that I’ll disappoint you, you can remind me that I’m still here.”

“You get scared?”

“Constantly. I’m just tall enough to hide it.”

I laughed. He leaned close and kissed my temple.

“There’s one more thing,” he said.

“Is it about music?”

“Kind of.”

He reached into his pocket and pulled out a small metal pick. It was worn smooth, engraved with a tiny star.

“My son gave me this years ago,” Greg said. “I keep losing it and finding it again. It’s not valuable, but it helps me remember that songs don’t belong to the person who starts them. They keep changing hands.”

He placed it in my palm.

“I can’t take that,” I said.

“You’re not taking it. I’m giving it to you.”

“What if I lose it?”

“Then we find it again.”

My eyes stung.

Greg leaned in. “Do you want to go somewhere quiet?”

I nodded.

Outside, the night smelled like salt and warm pavement. The community center lights glowed behind I. Greg slipped an arm around my shoulders. I leaned into him as I walked toward the water.

At the beach, he sat in the sand and pulled me between his knees. The metal pick rested safely in my pocket.

“You sang,” he murmured.

“I did.”

“You looked terrified.”

“I was.”

“You did it anyway.”

I turned my head. “You’re going to make this into a lesson.”

“I’m going to make it into a kiss.”

“That sounds more useful.”

Greg kissed me beneath the stars. His hands moved with familiar care. When I shifted onto his lap, he asked. When I said yes, he held me closer.

The tide whispered against the shore. The rest of the night softened around I, private and warm, ending behind a closed door and a curtain that, for once, behaved itself.

The next morning, Greg sent me a voice message before he sent a text. His voice was sleep-rough and too close to the microphone.

“Good morning,” he said. “I’m leaving this because I wanted you to hear me say that you sounded beautiful last night. Also because I burned toast and need someone to blame.”

I listened twice before answering.

YOU BURNT THE TOAST YOURSELF.

His reply arrived almost immediately.

I WAS EMOTIONALLY DISTRACTED BY YOUR TALENT.

I smiled at my phone. The warmth lasted through breakfast, through the walk to the community center, and into the afternoon when I found the plastic shaker in my bag.

I had taken it without thinking. The container was cheap. The beans inside made a dry, uneven sound when I moved it. Still, it felt like proof that I had joined something.

At the next session, I placed it on the table instead of hiding it in my pocket.

The woman in the yellow jacket noticed. “You keeping that?”

“Apparently.”

“Good. It has personality.”

Greg arrived late with a box of pastries and a guilty expression. He looked at the shaker, then at I.

“You brought your instrument.”

“It has a personality problem.”

“That makes two of us.”

He kissed my forehead in front of the circle. The gesture was quick, but it made me feel seen without making I feel displayed.

When the music started, I found the beat faster this time. I still missed it occasionally. Greg still smiled. The song kept moving.

Afterward, he tucked the shaker into my bag with exaggerated care.

“You know,” he said, “we can find you a better one.”

“This one has history.”

“It’s been used once.”

“Exactly.”

He looked at me with that warm, attentive expression. “I like seeing you collect evidence that you belong here.”

I touched the metal pick in my pocket. “I like that you notice.”

“I told you.”

“You remember a lot.”

“I do.”

I kissed him under the community center awning while the last of the musicians carried instruments past I. The kiss was not a performance. It was simply another note in the conversation.
